concepts.name: A ransom
concepts.why: Wesleyan / Baptist (general atonement) and Reformed: the name picks the 'for many' of Matthew and Mark, but 1 Timothy 2:6 in the same concept says 'for all'. Which of many/all is meant is exactly where these readers part, so the name must not choose. 'Ransom' is the word in all seven passages and is a plain label. (Concept 39 has the same many/us-all pairing, but its name is the quotation of Isaiah 53:12 and its passages carry both words; see secondary_or_links.)

Secular scholar / Jewish reader of the Hebrew Bible: Jeremiah 34:17 shares the word 'freedom' but says the opposite of the name; the LORD 'proclaims freedom' as irony, freedom to fall by sword, plague and famine. It does not hold 'liberty to the captives'. Move it to concept 18 (No one to save them), where it is a hard word in its right place, so nothing dark is lost. Separately, 35 and 36 are the same sub-theme (see secondary_or_links).

note_fixes: Mark 16:16: the note is an exact quotation and stays, but the card must carry the Berean's own mark that this verse is in the longer ending (16:9-20), which some of the earliest manuscripts omit; a reader should not meet it on the same footing as Acts 2:38.

1 Peter 3:21: no wording change (the notes must stay exact), but note that the Berean's 'symbolizes' renders the Greek 'antitypon' (corresponding to / an antitype); the whole verse is shown, which is right, so do not shorten the note to either half.
concepts.why: Baptist / free church and Lutheran / Catholic / Orthodox: the label is plain and fair, but the eight passages are all ones that join baptism to salvation, forgiveness or the Spirit, so the readings that hold baptism follows faith, or is not what saves, have only Acts 10:47 and the second half of Mark 16:16 and 1 Peter 3:21. Add the two most-cited texts the concept lacks, one for each of the other readings: 1 Corinthians 1:17 ('Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel') and Acts 16:33 ('he and all his household were baptized at once'). On Mark 16:16 (Doug asked): its use is fair, provided it is marked. It is in the Berean's printed text and is received as Scripture by Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and most Protestant churches; it is not load-bearing here, because Acts 2:38, 22:16 and 1 Peter 3:21 say the same without it; and it cuts both ways (the condemnation falls on 'whoever does not believe', not on the unbaptized). But a secular scholar and a Reformed or Baptist reader will object to meeting a disputed ending unmarked in a site that holds to the original, so the marker is the condition. Check that the MACULA Greek base actually carries 16:9-20; if it brackets or omits it, the marker is mandatory rather than advisable.

concepts.name: He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world
concepts.why: Secular scholar and Wesleyan: the name is 2 Thessalonians 2:13, whose 'from the beginning' is a disputed reading (some manuscripts read 'as firstfruits'), and 'to be saved' is said only there. Ephesians 1:4-5 says chosen 'to be holy and blameless', Romans 8:29-30 'conformed to the image of His Son', Acts 13:48 'appointed for eternal life'. Ephesians 1:4 is firm and fits all six passages. For balance: Reformed and Lutheran readers will look for Romans 9:15-16 and 1 Peter 1:1-2 here; if they are added, add Acts 17:30 and John 12:32 beside 'Who wants everyone to be saved' so the pair stays level (6 against 6 now).

concepts.name: It is for freedom that Christ has set us free
concepts.why: Biblical-theological reader: 'If the Son sets you free' is John 8:36 alone; Romans 6:18 and 6:22 name no one who sets free (set free from sin), and Romans 8:21 is the creation set free. Galatians 5:1 names Christ and John 8:36 the Son, so the Galatians 5:1 sentence covers more of the passages and says no more than they do.

Secular scholar (original arbitrates): the Berean's Psalm 62:1 says 'finds rest' and 'comes from Him', and has no waiting; the name says 'I wait'. The other seven say wait or await. Psalm 62:2 already stands in concept 19.

Baptist / dispensational, Reformed and Catholic readers on the order of the last things: Revelation 12:10 says 'Now have come the salvation', in the present, not 'ready to be revealed in the last time', and the timing of that scene is among the most disputed in Revelation. Putting it under a last-time heading places it, whatever the closing line says. It stays in the secondary Kingdom entry, and could also sit in concept 21 (Revelation 7:10 and 19:1 are there already), where its words 'salvation ... of our God' belong.

secondary_or_links: SAME SUB-THEME NAMED TWICE (Doug asked), clearest first: concepts 35 and 36. 'To proclaim liberty to the captives' (chains, prisoners, Jubilee) and 'I broke the bars of your yoke' (yoke, bonds, shackles) are one sub-theme, release from bondage; Isaiah 58:6 already says chains and yoke together, and both end in the same prophets. Merge them, or keep both only if the yoke concept is made to hold what is distinct (the yoke as the burden of an oppressor). Next, 9 and 27: 'They cried out to the LORD, and He heard' and 'From all his troubles' are the same call-and-answer pattern (Psalm 34:6 and 34:17 say cried out, heard, delivered, exactly as Psalm 107:6 and 107:13 do; Psalm 50:15 and 91:15 are the same). Third, 19 and 20: 'My rock, my fortress, and my deliverer' and 'God my Savior; the God of my salvation' are both the psalmists' 'my ...' titles for God (Psalm 18:2 and 18:46 are two lines of the same psalm; 'Rock of my salvation' is in 19 and 'God of my salvation' in 20). Pairs checked and judged distinct: 1/12 (God fights for Israel vs. not by weapons), 3/13 (a formula vs. the arm as a figure), 8/37 (the Egypt comparison vs. gathering), 30/31 (go'el as God vs. as a relative; keeping them apart avoids claiming a pattern), 32/33 (whom He redeemed vs. through whom), 53/54.

ORDER of the contested pairs: in each of the three pairs (44-46 grace and faith then works; 49 then 50; 51 then 52) the side that Reformed, Lutheran and Baptist readers hold comes first, and the Wesleyan, Catholic and Orthodox side second. It is not a fault in any one place and the texts are level in number, but a Wesleyan or Orthodox reader will notice the pattern. Consider putting 50 before 49 so the order does not run the same way three times.

Concept 39 'He bore the sin of many' has the same many/all pairing as 34 (53:6 'us all', 53:11-12 and Hebrews 9:28 'many'). It can stay, since the name is the quotation of Isaiah 53:12 and the all-passage is in the concept; if the owner wants the two kept consistent, 'He bore our sins' (1 Peter 2:24) is level. Isaiah 53 beside Hebrews 9:28 and 1 Peter 2:24 is grouped on wording the New Testament verses themselves share, and no line says who the Servant is, which is acceptable.

Secondary 'Salvation -> Righteousness' holds only Psalm 98:2 and Isaiah 59:16, 61:10; the New Testament's own pairing of righteousness with faith (Romans 1:17, 3:22) is the missing sub-theme named below. Add them there if they do not become a core concept.

Links to other themes: nothing to change; the ten labels are plain and take no side. If a theme on faith, the law or the church exists, Faith and Law would be the natural eleventh and twelfth, since 33, 46, 54 and 56 turn on them.

Completeness of the opposite readings (checked per concept): 44 and 45 against 46 are level in numbers, but see the missing sub-theme 'justified by faith' below: James 2:24 'justified by his deeds and not by faith alone' stands in 46 with no passage in the theme that says justified by faith. A Lutheran, Reformed or Catholic reader will see that gap at once.

Last concept (61): meets the rule. Words of hope from within the theme (Isaiah 25:8, John 11:25, 1 Corinthians 15, 2 Timothy 1:10, Hebrews 2:14-15, Revelation 21:4); the hard words stand in 17, 18, 29, 41 and 42 and are not softened, and 60 gives no order of the last things once Revelation 12:10 is moved.

missing.sub_theme: A man is justified by faith apart from works of the law
missing.why: The crux for the Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic readers. The theme sets 'not by works' (44), 'believe' (45) and 'work out' (46) side by side, but its only 'justified' sentence is James 2:24, so the faith side lacks the texts it is most known by. Genesis 15:6 and Habakkuk 2:4 are in the same passages' words if the owner wants the Old Testament roots. If these are held in a Righteousness theme, link it here by name.

missing.sub_theme: You have fallen away from grace; otherwise you also will be cut off
missing.why: The Wesleyan reader's counterpart to 51 (No one can snatch them out of My hand). Concept 52 has only the conditional passages (if you hold firmly) and none that say a believer may fall away or be cut off, so the free-will reading has its weaker texts and the security reading its strongest. Hebrews 10:26-27 and 2 Peter 2:20-21 are of the same kind. These are the dark words of this pair and the rule is that nothing dark is left out.

missing.sub_theme: That you may know that you have eternal life
missing.why: Assurance is where Reformed, Baptist, Wesleyan and Catholic readers part alongside perseverance, and the texts plainly develop it (know / examine yourselves / the Spirit testifies). Only Hebrews 3:14 and 2 Peter 1:10 touch it now, inside 52.

The disciples ask the question of this whole theme and are answered 'with man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible'; Luke 13:23-24 ('will only a few be saved?') is the hard word that stands beside the hope of the closing concept. Both election and free-will readers appeal to these, and neither is in the outline, though 'salvation belongs to the LORD' (21) and 'Strive to enter' type words are needed for the hard side.
